sal.basis: Senior Financial Analyst / FP&A, ~8 yrs, Frankfurt, fixed base (Jahresbrutto, bonus excluded): about EUR 75,000 gross a year, i.e. EUR 6,240 a month on 12 payments. Not re-verified live (search budget exhausted, official and salary hosts blocked); from prior knowledge of 2024-2025 German recruiter guides (Robert Half, Hays, Michael Page) and StepStone data: senior FP&A / senior controlling roles at 5-10 yrs roughly EUR 65-85k nationally, with Frankfurt about 5-10% above the national level; FP&A managers roughly EUR 85-110k. German pay is quoted as gross per year, so per=year. f = 6,240 / 26,000 = 0.24, so Noura's 34,000 SAR expectation maps to about EUR 98k a year, the entry FP&A-lead band, and comfortably above the 2026 EU Blue Card threshold (EUR 50,700). Confidence: medium-low.

sensitive.notes: German CVs (Lebenslauf) still often carry a photo, but under the General Equal Treatment Act (AGG, 2006) employers cannot require one and many international firms ask for none, so photo is optional: we offer an optional photo slot and never require one. Date of birth, nationality and marital status used to sit in the CV's 'Persönliche Daten' block; they are now optional and risky under the AGG (age, origin), so we never ask; right to work is asked instead of nationality. gender = none: German ATS forms very often make a salutation (Anrede: Frau / Herr / divers / keine Angabe) mandatory, but the engine's 'ask' renders a binary Female/Male 'Gender' question, which conflicts with the German 'divers' norm (BVerfG 2017, PStG 2018; OLG Frankfurt 2022 held a binary-only salutation choice in an online form discriminatory under the AGG). So we don't ask up front; a required Anrede is left for the user to pick on the form. Switch back to 'ask' only once the engine renders it as Anrede with Frau / Herr / divers / keine Angabe. Forms also routinely ask for expected salary (Gehaltsvorstellung) and earliest start date (Eintrittstermin); these are normal, not sensitive. The EU Pay Transparency Directive (transposition due 7 Jun 2026) bars asking for pay history, so we never fill current salary.

privacy.en: Your data is protected under the GDPR (DSGVO) and Germany's Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), and your CV only goes to employers you apply to.
privacy.ar: بياناتك محمية بموجب اللائحة العامة لحماية البيانات (GDPR/DSGVO) والقانون الاتحادي الألماني لحماية البيانات (BDSG)، ولا تُرسل سيرتك الذاتية إلا إلى جهات العمل التي تتقدّم إليها.
privacy.fr: Vos données sont protégées par le RGPD (DSGVO) et la loi fédérale allemande sur la protection des données (BDSG), et votre CV n'est transmis qu'aux employeurs auprès desquels vous postulez.

culture.notes: Mon-Fri, 38-40 hour week; hybrid with 2-3 office days is common at Frankfurt banks and corporates. Pay is discussed as gross per year (Jahresbrutto) and paid monthly at month end; many employers add a 13th salary or Christmas bonus, and banks add a variable bonus. Statutory employee notice is only 4 weeks to the 15th or the end of a month (s. 622 BGB), but contracts for experienced finance staff usually set 3 months to the end of a month or quarter; '6 weeks to quarter end' is also common, and probation is up to 6 months with 2 weeks' notice. So applications routinely ask for the earliest start date (frühestmöglicher Eintrittstermin) and expected salary (Gehaltsvorstellung), and hiring cycles are long. CV (Lebenslauf): tabular, reverse chronological, 1-2 pages; photo optional; signature and date no longer needed. A tailored cover letter (Anschreiben) is still expected by many traditional employers, though more firms now accept applications without one. Employer references (Arbeitszeugnisse) and degree certificates are often attached. Fluent German (C1) is required at most domestic employers; Frankfurt banks, Big Four and Berlin/Munich tech often work in English. Regulated roles at banks may ask for a certificate of good conduct (Führungszeugnis).
